description: I plan to build an AI-powered web dashboard for NASA's microgravity combustion research. It will summarize, rank, and compare investigations from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database, helping users find the results most relevant to fire safety in spacecraft and lunar habitats. Every AI summary will link to its source investigation, so users can check what the data actually supports.
summary:
NASA has flown dozens of fire experiments on the International Space Station, but the results are buried in long records and test tables that name their columns and units differently. Comparing two experiments means reading both by hand.

Entropy puts them in one table you can search and compare. For each experiment it shows 12 facts, like fuel, oxygen, pressure, airflow and sensors, and every value links back to the exact NASA sentence or table line it came from. An AI model reads each NASA record and suggests the values with a word-for-word quote, then our code checks that the quote really appears in NASA's text. If it doesn't, the cell says "Not stated" instead of guessing.

The catalogue covers the 19 investigations named in the challenge, and any other PSI investigation can be added live in about 10 seconds. I checked 55 values by hand against NASA's pages and 53 were correct.

Fire is one of the gravest risks on a spacecraft. Entropy makes NASA's fire-safety evidence easier to compare and trace.
details:
THE PROBLEM

Fire is one of the gravest risks on a spacecraft: there is nowhere to escape to, and without gravity flames behave in ways ground tests do not predict. NASA has run dozens of microgravity combustion experiments, but their results sit in long Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) records and test tables that name the same quantities differently and use different units. Comparing two experiments means reading both by hand.

WHAT ENTROPY DOES

Entropy turns those records into one comparable table with 12 facts per investigation: name, type, objectives, fire-safety pillar (prevention, detection or suppression), fuel or material, sample, oxygen, pressure, airflow, hardware and sensors. Its rule is simple: no proof, no value. Every value opens the NASA sentence or test-table line it came from, with a link to the PSI record. A value without proof reads "Not stated".

WHAT YOU CAN DO WITH IT

- Search and filter the 19 investigations named in the Flame in Freefall challenge (ACME, BASS, BASS-II, CFI, DAFT, FLEX, FLEX-2, SAFFIRE I to III, SAME, SAME-R, SLICE, SPICE and others).

- Compare 2 to 4 investigations and see what is the same, what differs and what NASA does not state.

- Add live: type any PSI investigation ID and watch its row fill in about 10 seconds, each value appearing only after it passes verification. Live rows are marked Unreviewed and are not saved.

- Ask Entropy: ask a question in plain words. An AI model only works out what you are asking; code computes the answer from the catalogue, and every value in it links to its NASA source.

- Tested atmospheres: a chart of the 747 NASA tests that record both oxygen and pressure, set against the three crew atmospheres NASA names in the PSI-20 record (14.7 psia with 21% oxygen, 10.2 psia with 26.5%, 8.2 psia with 34%). 182 tests sit near ISS cabin air, 6 near 10.2 psia, and none inside the zone around 8.2 psia with 34% oxygen. The closest is a PSI-159 test at about 0.5 atm and 34% oxygen.

- ISS cabin comparison: every stated oxygen and pressure value is tagged against station air (21% oxygen at 14.7 psia, from a NASA technical brief), and a filter shows the experiments run with more oxygen than the station. It compares conditions. It is not a fire-risk score.

- Experiment view: a 3D schematic of an investigation built only from its stated values. Parts NASA does not state stay grey, and selecting a part shows its source quote. It is not to scale and not a simulation, and no flame is drawn.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Fetch the PSI investigation record and its experimental-table CSV files.

2. Code summarizes each table: the minimum and maximum of every numeric column and the distinct values of short text columns, with the units exactly as NASA wrote them. Nothing is converted.

3. A large language model reads the record and proposes a value and a supporting quote for each field.

4. Code keeps a value only if its quote appears in NASA's text and the value appears inside the quote. The model never has the last word. The Objectives column is a written summary and the Pillar column is a classification; both are labelled as such.

HOW I CHECKED IT

I checked 55 values across 5 investigations by hand against their NASA PSI pages. The first review found 3 errors. I fixed their causes (fuel names stored in text columns of the test tables, and a flow rate placed in the airflow field), re-extracted the data and re-checked every changed value. Result: 53 of 55 correct. The two wrong cells (PSI-159 Pillar and Fuel) are named on the site. The code check is a text match: it traces a value to its source but does not prove the science, and the sample does not establish the accuracy of the whole catalogue.

WHAT IS CREATIVE ABOUT IT

Most tools ask users to trust an AI answer. Entropy lets the user check it: every value carries its own proof, and the system says "Not stated" instead of guessing. The same pipeline reads any PSI investigation, so the atlas can grow without hand work.

FACTORS I CONSIDERED

- Traceability over fluency: a value with no proof is shown as missing.

- No unit conversion, so NASA's numbers are never distorted. Odd values, such as the 2100% oxygen written in one NASA table, are shown as written with a "Check source" note.

- No invented risk score: NASA's records give none, so Entropy compares conditions only.

- Honest limits: text-match verification, a hand-checked sample, and the limits are written on the site.

- Respect for the data source: read-only requests made one at a time, and each record's own licence stated.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Researchers and spacecraft fire-safety engineers can compare fire experiments side by side instead of reading each record, trust each value because its source is one click away, and extend the atlas to new investigations in seconds.

WHAT COMES NEXT

All 133 PSI investigations, exports of sourced comparisons for spacecraft material and cabin safety reviews, researcher review marks so the verified part keeps growing, and NASA's own flame images and videos attached to each experiment.

TOOLS

TypeScript and Node.js; Hono for the API; Vite for the dashboard; three.js for the 3D experiment view; a large language model through its API for extraction; Vitest for 235 automated tests; hosted on Vercel; source code on GitHub under the MIT license.
